en: §1 Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:

§2 1) What, O Venerable Blessed One, is the root of merit (*kuśalamūla*) from the offering of a broom? 2) What is [the merit] from the offering of a mandala? 3) What is [the merit] from the training precepts of going for refuge to the Three Jewels? 4) What is [the merit] from the act of joining one’s palms in homage to the Tathāgatas? 5) What, O Venerable Blessed One, is the root of merit that is not exhausted nor depleted in *saṃsāra*, and which leads to the inexhaustible *nirvāṇa*? 6) What is [the merit] from the fashioning of an image of the Tathāgata?

The Blessed One said: "Ānanda, there are five benefits in the act of sweeping. What are the five? Namely: one's own mind becomes serene; the minds of others become serene; the deities become joyful; one performs and accumulates karma that leads to a pleasing appearance; and after the dissolution of the body, one is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world among the gods."

§4. Ānanda, whoever with a serene mind constructs a square mandala dedicated to the Tathāgata, for him, Ānanda, I declare the continent of Uttarakuru as the basis for sovereignty and lordship. Upon the dissolution of the body, he is reborn among the Trāyastriṃśa gods. §5. Ānanda, whoever with a serene mind constructs a semi-circular mandala dedicated to the Buddha, the Blessed One, for him, Ānanda, I declare the continent of Pūrvavideha as the basis for sovereignty and lordship. Upon the dissolution of the body, he is reborn among the Yāma gods.

§6. Ānanda, whoever makes a circular mandala dedicated to the Tathāgata, for him, Ānanda, I declare the continent of Aparagodānīya as the domain of sovereignty and lordship. Upon the dissolution of the body, he is reborn among the Tuṣita devas. §7. Ānanda, whoever makes a cart-shaped mandala dedicated to the Buddha, for him, Ānanda, I declare the continent of Jambūdvīpa as the domain of sovereignty and lordship. Upon the dissolution of the body, he is reborn among the Nirmāṇarati devas.

§8 Ānanda, whoever goes for refuge to the Buddha, goes for refuge to the Dharma, and goes for refuge to the Saṅgha, and having undertaken the five precepts, maintains them—I declare, Ānanda, that the root of merit of such a person is immeasurable and incalculable. It is not possible for Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas to grasp its limit; I declare it to extend even unto the end of Nirvāṇa.

§9 Then the Blessed One, knowing with his own mind the thought in the mind of the venerable Ānanda, covered his entire face up to the hairline with his broad and long tongue—which was like the pure, stainless, soft petals of a red lotus, and resembled a thin copper band free from the shoots of *kiṃśuka* or *aśoka*—and said to Ānanda: "Have you ever seen, Ānanda, such a radiant tongue as this belonging to anyone who is a liar, a slanderer, a speaker of harsh words, or a chatterer of idle talk? "No, Venerable Sir.
"For, Ānanda, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones are speakers of truth."

§10 "Ānanda, whichever beings, having joined their palms, shall perform an act of homage, saying, ‘Homage, homage to that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One,’ those beings have been taken into my care and brought to final nirvāṇa by me. I am not concerned for the welfare of those beings. Why is that? Because, Ānanda, the dharmadhātu of the Tathāgata is well-established."

Because it is so well-established, even the mere act of joining his palms does not go to waste, let alone the performance of acts such as giving. Behold, Ānanda, whatever belongs to that person—even if it is merely the rinsing water from a ladle, or the rinsing water from a bowl, or the rinsing water from a cooking pot—if he, with such a mind, were to pour it into an ant-hill, thinking, "May those living beings who depend upon this find happiness through this," then [the merit thereof would be immeasurable].

"Even this, Ānanda, I call a gateway to merit; how much more so for one who has become human! §11 There are these three intermediate kalpas, Ānanda. Which three? The intermediate kalpa of weapons, the intermediate kalpa of disease, and the intermediate kalpa of famine. In that regard, Ānanda, he who has undertaken and maintained the abstention from taking life for even a single day will not be reborn during the intermediate kalpa of weapons. He who has offered even a single myrobalan fruit to the Saṅgha will not be reborn during the intermediate kalpa of disease."
Whoever has given even a single spoonful of alms-food to the Saṅgha will not be reborn during an intermediate kalpa of famine.

§12 “Ānanda, there are these three roots of merit that are not exhausted and do not come to an end within saṃsāra, and they lead to the inexhaustible nirvāṇa. What are the three? Ānanda, a root of merit planted in the Buddha is not exhausted and does not come to an end within saṃsāra, and it leads to the inexhaustible nirvāṇa. A root of merit planted in the Dharma and a root of merit planted in the Saṅgha are not exhausted and do not come to an end within saṃsāra, and they lead to the inexhaustible nirvāṇa.”

§13 Then the Blessed One, for the purpose of manifesting the qualities of a Tathāgata, said: "Ānanda, have you seen the continent of Jambudvīpa? Ānanda replied: "I have seen it, Venerable Sir, the continent of Jambudvīpa. The Blessed One said: "It is seven thousand yojanas in length and seven thousand yojanas in width; it is broad in the north and shaped like a cart in the south."

Suppose some faithful son of good family or daughter of good family were to construct an image of him made of the seven precious gems and offer it to the community of monks from the four directions—consisting of stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas.
(Note: CUL manuscript reads *saṃghāya vihāraṃ niryātayet*; furthermore, the word *samantāt* is missing in the Potala manuscript.)

Or, whoever might establish for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly awakened one who has passed into parinirvāṇa, a stūpa made from a lump of clay the size of an *āmalaka* fruit, erect a staff the thickness of a needle, place a parasol the size of a jujube leaf, have an image fashioned the size of a barley grain, or deposit a relic the size of a mustard seed—for this, I declare, is a far greater merit than that.
§15 “Let alone, Ānanda, the continent of Jambūdvīpa. There is, Ānanda, a continent named Pūrvavideha, eight thousand yojanas in length and eight thousand yojanas in width, shaped like a half-moon.

Suppose some faithful son of good family or daughter of good family were to make it out of the seven precious gems and offer it to the stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas, and to the Saṅgha of monks from the four directions.”

Or, whoever might establish for a Tathāgata, Arhat, perfectly enlightened Buddha who has entered final nirvāṇa a stūpa made from a lump of clay the size of an *āmalaka* fruit, erect a staff as thin as a needle, place a parasol the size of a jujube leaf, fashion an image the size of a barley grain, or deposit a relic the size of a mustard seed—I declare that this latter merit is far more abundant than the former.
§17 Let alone Jambūdvīpa, Ānanda; let alone Pūrvavideha Island. There is, Ānanda, Aparagodānīya Island, nine thousand yojanas in length and nine thousand yojanas in width, shaped like the full moon.

Suppose some faithful son of good family or daughter of good family were to make it out of the seven precious gems and offer it to the stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas, as well as to the Saṅgha of monks from the four quarters.

Or, whoever might establish for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened one who has entered parinirvāṇa, a stūpa made from a lump of clay the size of an *āmalaka* fruit; erect a staff as thin as a needle; set up a parasol the size of a jujube leaf; have an image fashioned the size of a barley grain; or deposit a relic the size of a mustard seed—I declare that this latter merit is far more abundant than the former.

"Let alone, Ānanda, the continent of Jambūdvīpa; let alone the continent of Pūrvavideha; let alone the continent of Aparagodānīya. There is, Ānanda, a continent named Uttarakuru, ten thousand yojanas in length and ten thousand yojanas in breadth, square on all sides."

If some faithful son of good family or daughter of good family were to fashion an image of him out of the seven precious gems and offer it to the community of monks from the four directions—consisting of stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas—then [the merit would be great].

Or, whoever might establish for a Tathāgata, Arhat, perfectly enlightened Buddha who has entered final nirvāṇa a stūpa made from a lump of clay the size of an *āmalaka* fruit, erect a staff as thin as a needle, place a parasol the size of a jujube leaf, have an image fashioned the size of a barley grain, or deposit a relic the size of a mustard seed—for this, I declare, there is far greater merit than that.

§21 Let alone, Ānanda, the continent of Jambudvīpa; let alone the continent of Pūrvavideha; let alone the continent of Aparagodānīya; let alone the continent of Uttarakuru. There is, Ānanda, a palace of Śakra, the lord of the gods, named Vaijayanta.

Suppose some faithful son of good family or daughter of good family were to construct it out of the seven precious gems and offer it to the stream-enterers, the once-returners, the non-returners, the arhats, and the pratyekabuddhas, as well as to the Saṅgha of monks from the four quarters.

Or, whoever might erect for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly awakened one who has passed into parinirvāṇa, a stūpa made from a lump of clay the size of an *āmalaka* fruit, set up a staff as thin as a needle, place a parasol the size of a jujube leaf, have an image fashioned the size of a barley grain, or deposit a relic the size of a mustard seed—for this, I declare that there is even greater merit than the former.

"Let alone, Ānanda, the continent of Jambūdvīpa; let alone the continent of Pūrvavideha; let alone the continent of Aparagodānīya; let alone the continent of Uttarakuru; let alone Śakra, the lord of the gods, and his palace named Vaijayanta. There exists, Ānanda, a trichiliocosm, a great thousandfold world system."

If some faithful son of good family or daughter of good family were to fashion an image of him out of the seven precious gems and offer it to the community of monks from the four directions—consisting of stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas;

Or, whoever might establish for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly awakened one who has passed into parinirvāṇa, a stūpa made from a lump of clay the size of an *āmalaka* fruit, set up a staff the thickness of a needle, place a parasol the size of a *badarī* leaf, have an image fashioned the size of a barley grain, or deposit a relic the size of a mustard seed—for this I declare that there is far greater merit than that.

For what reason? Ānanda, the Tathāgata is immeasurable in his generosity, immeasurable in his ethical discipline, immeasurable in his patience, immeasurable in his vigor, immeasurable in his meditative concentration, and immeasurable in his wisdom.

[CUL adds: He is immeasurable in his loving-kindness, immeasurable in his compassion, immeasurable in his sympathetic joy, and immeasurable in his equanimity. He is immeasurable in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.

He is immeasurable by virtue of the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the three unique applications of mindfulness, and great compassion; Ānanda, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha is endowed with immeasurable qualities indeed—immeasurable, immeasurable, with a multitude of immeasurable qualities. While this Dharma discourse was being spoken, this trichiliocosm world-system trembled, shook, and quaked violently.
Then the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, what is the name of this Dharma-discourse? And how should I remember it?

The Blessed One said: "Therefore, Ānanda, you should remember this Dharma-discourse as 'The Drum of the Deathless' (Amṛtadundubhi), and you should also remember it as 'The Discourse on the Marvelous Dharma' (Adbhutadharmaparyāya). For that reason, 'The Discourse on the Marvelous Dharma' is also a designation for this Dharma-discourse."
Thus spoke the Blessed One; the Venerable Ānanda and those monks, being uplifted in mind, rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The second discourse, the Kūṭāgāra-sūtra, is finished.
